locus: Chow p.11-13 (CSE/PEOU); VLE F1 threshold-foreclosure / F7 presence-and-the-WE
note: (P/anticipatory-application) Chow's finding that computer self-efficacy is the strongest total predictor of self presence (0.53) offers an individual-determinant lens on vle-01's F1 threshold-foreclosure (install/hardware friction gating VID-stratum access) and its F7 presence-and-the-WE finding (self-report presence far higher in APP than VID stratum): low CSE may explain part of why some students never clear the installer gate, independent of the technology-side friction vle-01 documents directly.

target: Part III dissertation (self-efficacy as an unmeasured covariate)
note: (P/anticipatory-application) Part III's own deployment survey does not measure computer self-efficacy; Chow's SEM result (CSE's total effect on presence = 0.53, more than double PU's 0.36) suggests self-efficacy is a plausible unmeasured confound behind Part III's APP/VID stratification, worth flagging as a limitation rather than resolving.

target: Part III dissertation (self presence vs. the 'WE')
note: (P/anticipatory-application) Chow's narrow focus on self presence (avatar-as-self) rather than social presence (co-presence with others) sharpens Part III's F7 finding that VLE students wanted more 'watching with others': F7's gap is a social/co-presence phenomenon Chow's own model does not test, cautioning against reading Chow's self-presence determinants as if they explained social presence too.

Chow's actual dependent variable is Lee's (2004) 'self presence' — a virtual self experienced as the actual self — operationalized via three avatar-movement items (own avatar walking/moving/being in the ward); PU and CSE jointly explain 52% of its variance (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.2, p.11-12). Source's own term is 'presence'/'self presence'; normalized here to the embodiment/self-representation row since the instrument items are avatar-identification items, not spatial or social items.

Computer self-efficacy (CSE) — belief in one's ability to perform a specific task with the technology — is modeled as both a direct antecedent of perceived usefulness and a direct antecedent of self presence; it is the single strongest total predictor of presence in the model (total effect 0.53) (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.7, p.11, p.13).

Not modeled as an SEM variable; invoked post-hoc in the Discussion via Sweller's (1988) cognitive load theory to explain CSE's dominant effect — students with low computer self-efficacy expend cognitive resources on navigating the unfamiliar Second Life interface, leaving fewer resources for immersion (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.12).

Treated only as typological backdrop: Chow reproduces Lee's (2004) physical/social/self tripartite division of presence in the literature review before narrowing the study's own focus to self presence exclusively; physical presence itself is not modeled or measured (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.2).

Also typological backdrop only: Lee's social-presence type (a virtual social actor experienced as an actual social actor) is defined but explicitly set aside — Chow states the study's focus is self presence, not social presence, given the increase in avatar-based self-representation (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.3). Distinguishing this exclusion matters for Strand F, whose CMC-tradition sources treat social presence as their own primary construct.

Mentioned only in the literature-review synthesis of prior presence-and-learning findings (deByl 2009): presence in situated virtual worlds is said to nurture intrinsic motivation to learn beyond cognitive gain; this claim is not tested by Chow's own SEM, which contains no affect or motivation construct (FE, p.3, reporting others' findings, qualified as lit-review-only by this unit).

Named as one of the two 'media characteristics' determinant categories (media form: sensory fidelity, spatial-temporal match, interactivity) in the study's own two-category determinants-of-presence framework, then explicitly set aside as already well-studied so the paper can focus on the understudied user-characteristics category instead (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.3-4).

The PPE-selection-and-donning simulation is designed as a procedural-skills training platform (with an automated post-task performance log), and the literature review cites prior findings linking presence to learning outcomes generally; but Chow's own study collects no skills-assessment or performance-outcome data — presence is the sole dependent variable measured (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.4-6, p.7; design intent only, not an outcome finding).

The study's sole condition: a custom-built Second Life virtual ward and dressing-room simulation for PPE selection/donning, accessed via desktop (no HMD); avatar-mediated, screen-viewed. No comparison condition (e.g., 2D video, in-person) is included in the design (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.5-7).

Two-step SEM (measurement model then structural model, AMOS 19.0) is the study's entire analytic strategy; no between-media or between-group contrast is tested — the model explains variance within a single desktop-3D condition (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.9-12).
'The degree to which a user perceives the demands of significant others on him/her to use the technology,' adapted from Taylor & Todd (1995) via the TAM tradition (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.7).
'The extent to which a user views the usage of the technology to be relatively free of effort,' from Davis (1989)/Venkatesh & Davis (2000) (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.7).
'A user's belief about his/her ability to perform a specific task using the technology,' adapted from Vijayasarathy (2004) (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.7).
'The degree to which a user views the technology as offering better value than alternative methods of carrying out the same task,' from Davis (1989) (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.7).

target: Nature and Determinants of Presence Model / NDPM (TERM)
note: Dunnington's (2012) grounded-theory model of presence among nursing students in high-fidelity human patient simulation, positing pedagogical, individual, and group factors as determinants of a 'centricity' of presence, which in turn shapes learning outcomes; Chow's own four-variable model (SN, PEOU, CSE, PU) is presented as a simplified, testable instantiation of the NDPM's individual and group determinant categories (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.6-7).

Dunnington's term for the locus of a participant's state of being between simulation and physical environments, ranging from endocentricity (centered in the virtual) to exocentricity (centered in the physical); reported by Chow but not itself measured in this study's own instrument (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.6).
'A psychological state in which a virtual self is experienced as the actual self in either sensory or nonsensory ways,' from Lee (2004); the study's sole dependent construct (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.2).

The three-item presence scale asks whether respondents felt as if they themselves were walking/moving/inside the ward when their avatar walked/moved/visited — an embodiment-through-motor-correspondence operationalization adapted from Jin & Park's (2009) Wii avatar-interaction scale (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.7-8).

Ten single-patient treatment rooms, each with a donning/doffing anteroom; avatars must read a patient record, select correct PPE items in sequence, and complete a system-logged performance record — the study's own custom-built stimulus environment (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.5-6).

Chow cites the author's own prior work (Chow, Herold, Choo & Chan 2012) — a Second Life virtual ward for practising rapid sequence intubation — as a precedent healthcare-simulation design, establishing continuity between this study and the author's earlier TAM-based Second Life healthcare-education work (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.3).

Chow opens the concept-of-presence literature review with Lombard & Ditton's (1997) six explications and their 'perceptual illusion of non-mediation' definition, the same source built in this cluster as ped-sec-01 (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.2, quoting Lombard & Ditton p.9).

Source of the physical/social/self tripartite presence typology and the general definition of presence as virtual objects experienced as actual objects; Chow adopts self presence as the study's focus construct from this typology (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.2).
Cited for the claim that presence is a human reaction to immersion, distinguishing immersion (an objective system property) from presence (a subjective response) (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.2).

Cognitive load theory (1988) supplies the Discussion's explanation for computer self-efficacy's dominant effect on presence: low-CSE users spend extraneous cognitive resources navigating the interface rather than immersing in the activity (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.12).

Originator of the Technology Acceptance Model (1989), source of the perceived-usefulness/perceived-ease-of-use belief pair that Chow imports wholesale as the study's own core mechanism linking presence determinants to presence (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.6-7).

Author of the Nature and Determinants of Presence Model (NDPM, 2012 dissertation; 2014 journal article), the grounded-theory framework Chow's own research model is explicitly derived from (FAITHFUL-Chow, p.6).

Cited only as one of several 'key authors of presence' supporting the determinants/centricity/outcome framing; this is Witmer & Singer's 2005 factor-structure follow-up paper, not the 1998 Presence Questionnaire paper built in this cluster as ped-sec-02 — Chow never cites the 1998 PQ paper itself, a discrepancy worth flagging (FE, p.6, cross-checked against ped-sec-02's citation).

locus: Chow p.3-4 (determinants-of-presence framework); cf. Witmer & Singer 1998 section 3 Contributing Factors
note: (P/anticipatory-application) This cluster's own debate-axis-3 construction, not a claim either source makes about the other. Witmer & Singer's Control/Sensory/Distraction/Realism categories exemplify the technology-determined pole; Chow's explicit two-category split (media characteristics vs. user characteristics) and single-minded focus on the empirically neglected user-characteristics side — SN, PEOU, CSE, PU, none of them technology properties — instantiate the psychologically/individually-determined pole. Chow does not cite Witmer & Singer's 1998 PQ paper directly (see the Witmer/Jerome/Singer-2005 cites edge above), so this opposition is this cluster's own alignment of the two units, not an authorial cross-reference.
